While that my soul repairs to her devotion, Here I intomb my flesh, that it betimes May take acquaintance of this heap of dust; To which the blast of death's incessant motion, Fed with the exhalation of our crimes, Drives all at last. Therefore I gladly trustMy body to this school, that it may learn To spell his elements, and find his birth Written in dusty heraldry and lines ; Which dissolution sure doth best discern, Comparing dust with dust, and earth with earth. These laugh at jet, and marble put for signs,To sever the good fellowship of dust, And spoil the meeting. What shall point out them, When they shall bow, and kneel, and fall down flat To kiss those heaps, which now they have in trust? Dear flesh, while I do pray, learn here thy stem And true descent: that when thou shalt grow fat,And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know, That flesh is but the glass, which holds the dust That measures all our time; which also shall Be crumbled into dust. Mark, here below, How tame these ashes are, how free from lust, That thou mayst fit thyself against thy fall.

**A Polished Rendering**

While my soul withdraws into devotion, I lay my flesh to rest here, that it might early make the acquaintance of this gathered dust—dust toward which the relentless breath of death, nourished by the vapors of our transgressions, inexorably drives us all. Gladly, then, do I commend my body to this solemn school, that it may learn to decipher its own elements and trace its origin, inscribed in the humble heraldry of dust and line. For dissolution alone can truly discern such kinship, weighing dust against dust, and earth against earth.

These modest remains hold in quiet contempt the pretensions of jet and marble monuments, erected to sunder the true fellowship of dust and disrupt its reunion. Yet what, in the end, will distinguish the proud, when they themselves must bow, kneel, and prostrate themselves to kiss these very heaps now placed in their keeping?

Beloved flesh, even as I pray, learn here your lineage and true descent—so that when you grow full and restless with desire, you may remember that flesh is but the fragile vessel containing the dust by which all our time is measured, a vessel destined itself to crumble into dust. Observe, then, how peaceful these ashes lie, how utterly free from craving, that you may prepare yourself, in humility, for your own eventual fall.

I entomb my flesh among the dead, and there let it lie, while my soul ascends to its proper devotions. For it seems fitting—indeed, necessary—that the body should grow acquainted, even now, with the dust into which it must one day dissolve. What better preparation for that final transformation than to dwell, in thought and in practice, upon the very substance to which all flesh returns?

For all human life, from its first breath to its last, is driven relentlessly by death toward this common heap of dust. No rank, no fortune, no earthly distinction stays this march. It is a fate hastened and fed, moreover, by the corruption of human sin, which taints our nature and hurries us all the more swiftly toward that final dissolution. We are, each of us, travelers upon the same road, though we may deceive ourselves into thinking otherwise.

Knowing this, I willingly commit my body to the grave as to a school—a place of humble instruction where flesh may learn what words and reason alone cannot teach it. There, in the quiet company of the dead, dust may be compared with dust, and earth measured against earth, until the body comes to know, in its very substance, its true origin and its certain end. This is no morbid indulgence, but a necessary education, one that the living too often neglect until it is thrust upon them by death itself.

And what, then, of those monuments we raise to distinguish the dead—the gleaming marble, the polished jet, the carved inscriptions that promise remembrance and rank even in the tomb? These I hold to be nothing more than vain and foolish attempts to separate what death has already made equal. For beneath the stone and beneath the sculpted name, all bodies dissolve into the same substance, all join the same "fellowship of dust." No monument, however grand, can preserve distinction where nature itself insists on unity. Death is the great leveler, and its kingdom knows no hierarchy.

Therefore, I urge my own flesh to learn this lesson now, while there is yet time to profit from it. Let it not wait until the moment of death to discover what it is. For when pride swells within me, or when the body grows indulgent in its pleasures and forgetful of its frailty, let this knowledge return—that I am dust, and to dust I shall return. In remembering this humble origin, I may temper my vanities, restrain my appetites, and prepare myself calmly and without terror for that inevitable hour when flesh must finally keep the appointment dust has always promised.

# Expanding the Summary: A Devotional Poem on Mortality

## The Poem's Central Conceit

This meditative poem stages an extraordinary devotional exercise: the speaker deliberately entombs his own living flesh among the dust of the dead, transforming the grave into a pedagogical space—a "school" for the body. Rather than avoiding thoughts of death, the speaker actively seeks out proximity to decay, using the physical reality of human remains as a teaching tool. The body, still animated and full of worldly appetites, is brought face-to-face with its ultimate destination: disintegration into the same anonymous dust that fills every grave.

## The Lesson of "Dust with Dust, and Earth with Earth"

The poem's central pedagogical method involves a stark comparison—setting "dust with dust, and earth with earth"—which serves to strip away the illusions the body maintains about its own significance. By literally or imaginatively placing his flesh alongside decomposed remains, the speaker forces a confrontation with an uncomfortable truth: all human bodies, regardless of their former beauty, status, or vitality, become indistinguishable dust in the end. This lesson in humility operates through direct sensory and imaginative experience rather than abstract theological argument. The body must *learn* its origins and destiny not through intellectual assent alone, but through visceral encounter with the very substance it will become.

## Critique of Vain Monuments

Embedded within this meditation is a pointed critique of funerary monuments—jet, marble, and other costly materials used to mark and beautify graves. The poem suggests that such monuments represent a vain and ultimately futile attempt to distinguish the dead from common decay, to preserve status and individuality even in death. This critique serves the poem's larger argument: no ornament, however precious, can alter the fundamental truth that all flesh reduces to the same humble matter. The elaborate tomb, then, becomes an ironic symbol of the very pride and vanity the poem seeks to dismantle—an attempt to armor the body against its own inevitable humiliation.

## The Memento Mori Function

The poem's deepest significance lies in its function as a memento mori—a reminder of death designed to reshape the speaker's spiritual and moral orientation while he yet lives. By confronting the body directly with its future state of dissolution, the speaker aims to accomplish several interconnected devotional goals:

**Tempering pride**: If the flesh can be made to internalize, in advance, its coming reduction to dust, it may lose some of its inclination toward vanity, self-importance, and worldly ambition. The body that truly *knows* it will become anonymous earth has less grounds for arrogance.

**Curbing carnal desire**: Similarly, by envisioning the future ashes as entirely "lust-free"—stripped of all appetite, sensation, and desire—the speaker hopes to weaken the grip of carnal cravings in the present. The dust does not hunger, does not lust, does not seek pleasure; contemplating this future state serves as a check against present sensual indulgence.

**Spiritual preparation**: Ultimately, this exercise in anticipatory mortality serves a preparatory function. By rehearsing, in meditation, the body's fall into dust, the speaker seeks to ready his soul for that inevitable transition—approaching death not as a terrifying rupture but as a already-familiar destination, its lessons absorbed in advance through the discipline of contemplative practice.

## Conclusion

Through this unusual and intimate meditation—entombing the living body among the dead as an act of spiritual pedagogy—the poem transforms the grave from a site of horror into a site of instruction. Its critique of ostentatious monuments underscores the futility of resisting mortality through material means, while its central devotional aim remains the reformation of the flesh's present desires through vivid, disciplined contemplation of its future dissolution. In this way, the poem exemplifies the memento mori tradition's power to use death not merely as an object of fear, but as a resource for moral and spiritual transformation in life.

# While, Here, May

While the world spins forward in its relentless rhythm, we often forget to pause and notice the spaces between moments. Time moves whether we watch it or not, carrying us through days that blur together until we lose track of what mattered and what merely happened.

Here, in this particular moment, something different is possible. Here is not just a location but a state of attention—a choice to be present rather than lost in memory or anticipation. The word itself anchors us, reminding us that this exact point in space and time is the only one we can truly inhabit. Everything else is imagination or recollection.

May carries a double meaning that feels appropriate to this reflection. As a month, May represents renewal—the last threshold before summer, when spring's promises begin to bear fruit. Trees that seemed barely awake in March now stand fully dressed in green. But May also functions as a word of possibility, of permission, of uncertain futures: things that may happen, may change, may surprise us.

Together, these three words sketch a quiet philosophy. While time continues its march, we are invited to remain here, grounded in the present, even as we acknowledge that many things may unfold in ways we cannot yet imagine. This is not passivity but a kind of active patience—an openness to whatever comes while refusing to abandon the ground beneath our feet.

Perhaps this is the essence of mindful living: honoring the "while" of ongoing time, cherishing the "here" of immediate experience, and remaining curious about the "may" of unwritten possibility. In holding these three ideas together, we find a balance between motion and stillness, between what is fixed and what remains open.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphysical poem in the style of George Herbert about contemplating mortality inside a church tomb.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Vault

Here in this stone I lay me down to think
Upon the marble bed where others sleep,
Their names half-worn as letters seem to shrink
Like breath itself, too faint, too poor to keep.

The tomb's cold mouth speaks nothing, yet it saith
More than the preacher's voice from pulpit high:
*All flesh is grass* — the text of common death
Writ plain in dust, no need to wonder why.

Lord, teach my soul to read this alphabet
Of bone and epitaph, that I may spell
Some grace within the grave, some antidote set
Against the poison of my private hell.

For I do fear this house of narrow stone,
Yet fear is but my pride grown thin and pale;
I built a self I thought was mine alone,
Now see it crumble like a rented sail.

What if this darkness were a kind of door?
What if the worm that works were secret friend,
Unstitching what my vanity wore
That I might wear Thy garment in the end?

The tomb says: *nothing*. But Thy Word says: *wait* —
As seed must wait in earth's uncertain womb.
So let me lie, a pupil of my fate,
Content to learn my lesson in this room.

Then, Lord, if I must be a piece of ground,
Let me be ground Thou plantest, not just lost;
Let resurrection's key be somewhere found
Hung on the belt of this, my dearest cost.

So death, be not my period, but my pause —
A comma in the sentence of Thy grace,
Where I, unlearning all my broken laws,
Am rewrit wholly in another's face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a 17th-century-style devotional verse where the speaker addresses his own flesh, using dust and burial imagery to teach humility.
counterfactuals.output:
# Upon Mortality Considered

Poor flesh, why swell'st thou with such vain array,
As if thy substance were not brittle clay?
Thou that wast dust before thou breath'd the light,
And shalt be dust again ere long, ere night
Of death close o'er thee—wherefore then this pride,
This borrowed pomp that death shall soon divide?

Consider, soul-encased and mortal frame,
From whence thou cam'st, and whither goes thy name:
The earth first lent thee for a little space
This fashioned form, this temporary face,
And earth shall have her lease again full soon,
Not asking leave, nor waiting for the noon
Of thy desires, nor for thy summer's prime—
She calls her due at her appointed time.

What is this hand that now doth grasp for more,
But dust that shall lie still upon death's floor?
What is this eye that rolls in wanton glance,
But dust that in the grave shall have no chance
To see the sun, nor mark the morning's birth,
But keep close fellowship with mother earth?

Then, flesh, be humble—thou that art but lent,
A tenant here, not owner of thy tent.
The worm that now thou treadst beneath thy shoe
Shall be thy bedfellow, and prove it true
That crowns and rags alike to dust must fall,
And one thin shroud will serve to cover all.

Yet weep not, flesh, as though no hope remained—
The dust thou art shall not be always chained;
For He who formed thee first from common earth
Shall stoop again and give thee second birth,
And what went down corruptible and poor
Shall rise array'd, and die, O death, no more.

So till that day, walk softly, house of clay,
Remember well thou art but dust today;
Let not the borrowed breath thou now dost keep
Make thee forget how soon thou'lt fall asleep
Beneath the sod, where kings and beggars meet,
And pride lies humbled at the last complete.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a Metaphysical poem, similar to "Church-monuments," reflecting on death, decay, and the vanity of pride in the body?
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Frailty of This Borrowed Clay

Come, restless flesh, and learn thy lesson well
From marble tombs where lords and ladies dwell
In stone that mocks the very pride it holds—
For what is flesh but clay that time enfolds?

I saw a skull beneath a painted face,
A jeweled hand that time would soon erase,
And thought: this body, which I call my own,
Is but a tenant in a house of bone.

The proud man struts in silk and burnished gold,
Unknowing that his marrow groweth old,
That worms, more patient than his flattering friends,
Await the feast that every glory ends.

What is this pulse but time's own metronome,
Counting the steps that lead the body home—
Not to some palace built by mortal hands,
But to the dark, where dust reclaims its lands?

The mirror lies. It shows a fixed estate,
When flesh, in truth, is water at the gate,
Forever pouring toward that silent sea
Where kings and beggars share one entropy.

So let this thought be marrow to my bone:
That pride is but a tenant, death the own;
That every heartbeat is a step more near
The stone-cold truth that make the proudest fear.

Yet in this fear, O soul, thou mayst find rest—
For if the body's but a borrowed vest,
Then thou art more than what shall turn to dust:
A spark that flesh contains, but is not, just.

So mock me not, thou skull beneath my skin,
I'll wear thee lightly till the end begin,
And when the seams of flesh at last give way,
I'll shed this clay, and find eternal day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in iambic pentameter with irregular rhyme, echoing the tone of 17th-century religious poetry, about a soul preparing for death while the body awaits burial.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon the Soul's Departure**

My body lies, a lamp whose oil grows dim,
awaiting now the hand that snuffs the flame;
the worms prepare their solemn feast for him
who once was known and called by a warm name.
I feel the cold creep upward from my feet,
as winter climbs a tree it means to kill;
and yet in this last hour, Death, we meet
not quite as foes, but guests who share one will.

For Thou, O Lord, hast lent this house of clay
a little while, and now the lease is spent;
I do not grudge to give the rent away,
nor mourn the fall of this poor tenement.
The soul, Thy tenant, folds her slender store—
some faith, more failing than she'd wish to own—
and lifts her hand to knock upon the door
of that far country where she is not known.

Come, sexton, then, and dig where violets grow;
my eyes are strangers to the comfort here.
I was a bubble lifted high to show
a borrowed light not mine, though bright, though dear.
The color was but breath, the shine but loan;
now let it break, and let the breaking be
not loss, but going home, not final, but a stone
rolled from a door that was not sealed on me.

So loose the knot that ties this flesh to soul,
as one unmoors a boat too long delayed—
I do not know the harbor, nor the whole
dark voyage through; yet I am not afraid
past reason's edge, for reason cannot swim
so far as love has gone before, and stayed.

Receive me, Christ, not for what I have done,
whose ledger groans with debts I cannot pay,
but for the borrowed merit of the Son
who turned my midnight into lasting day.
Then bury me; this dust shall wait, not weep,
till trumpets wake what graves were meant to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate George Herbert's poetic voice and themes to write a meditation on mortality, using extended metaphors of dust, ashes, and the body as an hourglass.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Hourglass

My body is an hourglass of dust,
Which through the narrow neck of hours must
                    Let fall each grain
                    Of breath and pain,
Till all the upper chamber empties clean
And I lie flat, as though I'd never been.

The sand that now records my fleeting stay
Was rock and mountain in some other day;
                    God ground it small
                    To mark my fall
From breath to breath, from waking unto sleep,
That I might learn what hours I ought to keep.

Ashes to ashes—so the Preacher saith,
And dust to dust returns the borrowed breath.
                    Yet in the glass
                    The grains that pass
Fall not to loss, but to a lower place
Where Thou dost keep them, Lord, by Thy strange grace.

For Thou canst take the hourglass in Thy hand
And turn it over, make it new-made stand:
                    The dust that fell
                    Shall rise and tell
A second story, if Thou wilt but choose
To breathe again what death would have me lose.

So let me be, while yet my sand runs clear,
Not fixed on that dark moment drawing near,
                    But on the Hand
                    That wrought the sand,
That measures out my dust in love, not spite,
And turns my ashes into morning light.

Teach me to read the glass and not despair,
Since every falling grain's become Thy care;
                    And when the last
                    Sand-grain has passed,
Let me not fear the emptying of the frame,
But trust the Hand that gave it, and its name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
